Countries in Africa.Egypt: The pyramids of Giza are over 4,500 years old. Egypt spans two continents, with the Sinai in Asia.
Countries in Africa.Morocco: Home to the world's oldest continuously operating university, al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859.
Countries in Africa.Nigeria: Africa's most populous country, with over 200 million people, and home to its famous film industry, Nollywood.
Countries in Africa.Kenya: Famed for the wildebeest migration across the Masai Mara, and for its marathon runners.
Countries in Africa.Ghana: In 1957 it became the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from colonial rule.
Countries in Africa.Senegal: Dakar is its capital, the westernmost city on the African mainland, near the Pink Lake, Lac Rose.
Countries in Africa.Angola: Its second-largest city, Luanda, was once capital of Portuguese rule. Angola gained independence in 1975.
Countries in Africa.Madagascar: An island nation, most of whose species exist nowhere else on Earth, including all lemurs.
Countries in Africa.Namibia: Has the Namib, one of the world's oldest deserts, and its dunes meet the Atlantic Ocean at the Skeleton Coast.
Countries in Africa.Botswana: Home to the Okavango Delta, where a river flows into the desert and spreads out instead of reaching the sea.
Countries in Africa.Zambia: Victoria Falls, called Mosi-oa-Tunya or 'the smoke that thunders', is on its border with Zimbabwe.
Countries in Africa.Tunisia: Ancient Carthage lay near Tunis. Tunisia also gave a sandy planet its name in Star Wars, as Tatooine was filmed there.
Countries in Africa.Sudan: It once was Africa's largest country by area before South Sudan split in 2011. More pyramids stand there than in Egypt.
Countries in Africa.Libya: Most of its land is Sahara desert, and the country holds Roman ruins like Leptis Magna on the Mediterranean.
Countries in Africa.Yemen: Yemen is in Asia, on the Arabian Peninsula, and its capital Sana'a is famed for its tower houses.
Countries in Africa.Oman: A country in southwest Asia, known for frankincense, which the sultanate has traded for thousands of years.
Countries in Africa.Jordan: A West Asian country with Petra, a city carved into rose-red rock. It is not in Africa.
Countries in Africa.Syria: A country in Western Asia whose capital Damascus is among the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities.
Countries in Africa.Iraq: In Asia, ancient Mesopotamia, where writing was invented around 5,000 years ago.
Countries in Africa.Sri Lanka: An island nation off India's southern tip, in Asia, and a major producer of Ceylon tea.
Countries in Africa.Fiji: An archipelago of over 300 islands in the Pacific, in Oceania, not near Africa.
Countries in Africa.Papua New Guinea: In Oceania, it has over 800 languages, more than any other country.
Countries in Africa.Haiti: A Caribbean nation that in 1804 became the first republic founded by formerly enslaved people.
Countries in Africa.Guyana: A trap on the other side of the Atlantic: it is in South America, with a name from an indigenous word meaning 'land of many waters'.

Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Basil: A member of the mint family, it's the star of pesto, and holy basil, a relative, is sacred in India.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Parsley: Flat-leaf parsley has a stronger flavor than the curly kind that's sometimes just a garnish.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Cilantro: For some people, a gene variation (near OR6A2) makes this herb taste like soap.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Thyme: Its main oil, thymol, is a natural antiseptic that also appears in mouthwashes.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Rosemary: Its Latin name means 'dew of the sea', because the shrub thrives in coastal air.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Oregano: The Greek name means 'joy of the mountain', and it's the soul of pizza and Greek salad.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Sage: Its Latin root means 'to save', as ancient healers saw it as a cure-all.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Mint: It spreads wildly through underground runners, so gardeners often pot it to keep it contained.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Dill: The feathery leaves are the herb, while the seeds from the same plant count as a spice.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Chives: The smallest member of the onion family, and its flowers are edible too.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Tarragon: Its name goes back to a Latin word meaning 'little dragon', and it's the signature of béarnaise sauce.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Marjoram: A close cousin of oregano but sweeter and milder, it's often added late in cooking.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Bay leaf: Ancient Greeks crowned victors with laurel, but the cook usually removes it, since the leaf stays stiff.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Cumin: It's a seed, from the same dried cuminum plant used in curries and chili, so a spice rather than a leafy herb.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Cinnamon: This spice is dried bark, rolled into quills. Cassia is its common cheaper cousin.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Nutmeg: A seed with a warm aroma, it's a spice, and large doses can be toxic. Its covering is mace.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Turmeric: A root (turmeric is a rhizome), so a spice, and the source of yellow in curry.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Paprika: Dried ground red peppers, so a spice from the fruit rather than a leaf.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Clove: The dried flower bud of a tree, a spice that numbs the mouth, and was once worth gold.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Cardamom: A seed pod; this expensive spice is a seed, used in coffee in the Middle East.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Saffron: The red threads are the stigmas of a crocus, picked by hand; about 150 flowers yield one gram, so it is a spice, not a leafy herb.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Black pepper: Black pepper is the dried berry of a climbing vine, once so valuable it was used to pay rent and taxes.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Star anise: A star-shaped fruit pod from a Chinese tree, a spice, and a key flavor in pho and five-spice powder.
Herbs (the leafy kind not spices).Allspice: The dried unripe berry of a Caribbean tree, a spice, and it tastes like clove, nutmeg and cinnamon at once.

Chili pepper varieties.Jalapeño: Jalapeños are medium-hot and typically rank about 2,500 to 8,000 on the Scoville scale, and when dried and smoked they become chipotles.
Chili pepper varieties.Habanero: Habaneros are many times hotter than jalapeños, about 100,000 to 350,000 Scoville units, and have a fruity, floral flavor.
Chili pepper varieties.Serrano: Serrano peppers are small and thin-skinned, typically hotter than jalapeños, and they're a staple of fresh salsas in Mexico.
Chili pepper varieties.Cayenne: Cayenne peppers are thin, hot, and usually sold dried and ground, and the name comes from Cayenne in French Guiana.
Chili pepper varieties.Scotch bonnet: Scotch bonnets look like a tam o' shanter hat and are the signature Jamaican pepper, similar in heat to habanero.
Chili pepper varieties.Ghost pepper: The ghost pepper, or bhut jolokia, from northeastern India was once certified the world's hottest chili, at over a million Scoville units.
Chili pepper varieties.Carolina Reaper: Carolina Reaper, bred in South Carolina, held the Guinness record for hottest chili for years, averaging over 1.5 million Scoville units.
Chili pepper varieties.Thai chili: Thai chilies are tiny and sharp, often called bird's eye chilies, and are used in Southeast Asian curries.
Chili pepper varieties.Chipotle: A chipotle is just a smoke-dried jalapeño, and the name comes from a Nahuatl word for smoked chili.
Chili pepper varieties.Poblano: Poblano is a mild dark-green chili from Puebla, and when dried it's called an ancho.
Chili pepper varieties.Guajillo: Guajillo is a mild to medium dried chili with a fruity flavor, and it's the backbone of many Mexican red sauces.
Chili pepper varieties.Black pepper: Black pepper is from the dried fruit of a tropical vine, and it's not a chili pepper; Europeans named chilies 'pepper' by analogy.
Chili pepper varieties.Pink peppercorn: Pink peppercorns come from a different plant, in the cashew family, and unlike real pepper can trigger allergies in some nut-sensitive people.
Chili pepper varieties.Sichuan pepper: Sichuan pepper is the husk of a prickly ash berry, not a chili, and it creates a numbing tingle rather than burn.
Chili pepper varieties.White pepper: White pepper is black pepper's seed with the outer layer removed, so it's not a chili.
Chili pepper varieties.Wasabi: Wasabi's heat is a sharp vapor that hits the nose, and it comes from a different plant family, not a chili.
Chili pepper varieties.Horseradish: Horseradish is a root whose nasal-clearing sting comes from a compound different from capsaicin, so it's not a chili.
Chili pepper varieties.Ginger: Ginger is a rhizome whose heat comes from gingerol, and it has no relation to the chili family.
Chili pepper varieties.Mustard: Mustard seeds make heat through a reaction that creates volatile compounds when crushed with liquid, not through capsaicin.
Chili pepper varieties.Dr Pepper: Dr Pepper is a soda; there's no pepper in it, and the name's origin remains unclear.
Chili pepper varieties.Peppermint: Peppermint is a mint, a cooling herb, with no relation to chilies, whose menthol tricks the brain into feeling cold.
Chili pepper varieties.Radish: Radishes have a peppery bite from compounds like those in mustard, but they are no chilies.
Chili pepper varieties.Pepperoni: Pepperoni is an American spicy salami and takes its name from 'peperoni', the Italian word for bell peppers, not the pepper itself.
Chili pepper varieties.Green peppercorn: Green peppercorns are unripe black pepper berries, picked early, and they're not chilies.

Dumplings of the world.Gyoza: Japanese pan-fried dumplings, adapted from Chinese jiaozi after WWII. Pork, cabbage and garlic are the classic filling.
Dumplings of the world.Pierogi: Polish stuffed dumplings with potato, cheese, cabbage or fruit. They are a Christmas Eve staple, and in Polish the word is already plural.
Dumplings of the world.Momo: Steamed dumplings from Nepal and Tibet, often with yak or buffalo meat. Spicy tomato achar is the standard dip.
Dumplings of the world.Xiaolongbao: Shanghai soup dumplings, filled with meat and a gelatinized broth that melts inside as they steam. Careful of the burning first bite.
Dumplings of the world.Wonton: Cantonese dumplings with a thin wrapper, often served in broth. The name means swallowing clouds in Cantonese.
Dumplings of the world.Pelmeni: Small Russian and Siberian meat dumplings, traditionally frozen outdoors in winter as portable food for hunters.
Dumplings of the world.Mandu: Korean dumplings, steamed, fried or boiled. They are the key dish of the Lunar New Year soup, tteok-mandu guk.
Dumplings of the world.Har gow: A Cantonese dim sum dumpling with shrimp and a translucent wrapper. A good dim sum chef is judged on theirs.
Dumplings of the world.Khinkali: Georgian dumplings with a twisted top and soup inside. You hold them by the knob and don't eat it.
Dumplings of the world.Manti: Tiny Turkish dumplings boiled and served with yogurt and spicy butter. In Kayseri, a skilled cook fits dozens onto a spoon.
Dumplings of the world.Shumai: Open-topped steamed dumplings with pork and shrimp, a dim sum staple. The Japanese version comes with a pea on top.
Dumplings of the world.Matzo ball: A dumpling of matzo meal in chicken soup, a Jewish Passover and Ashkenazi comfort food. Debate rages over floaters versus sinkers.
Dumplings of the world.Spring roll: Rolled and fried, not a dumpling. The crisp wrapper makes it a roll.
Dumplings of the world.Empanada: A baked or fried turnover filled with meat or cheese. The name derives from the Spanish for wrapped in bread.
Dumplings of the world.Calzone: A folded pizza that's baked, closer to a pie than a dumpling. Its name means trouser leg in Italian.
Dumplings of the world.Egg roll: Deep-fried, thick-wrapped roll, an American Chinese invention. It is not dumpling.
Dumplings of the world.Taquito: Rolled and fried tortilla. The name means little taco.
Dumplings of the world.Croquette: Breaded fried filling, often potato or bechamel. Its name means to crunch in French.
Dumplings of the world.Falafel: Fried chickpea balls, not wrapped dough. Made from legumes, not dumplings.
Dumplings of the world.Onigiri: Rice balls and not dough. Onigiri is eaten with the fingers.
Dumplings of the world.Burrito: Tortilla wrapped around fillings. Its name means little donkey in Spanish.
Dumplings of the world.Cornish pasty: Baked pastry, once a miner's lunch. The thick crimped crust was a handle for dirty hands.
Dumplings of the world.Arancini: Fried rice balls from Sicily. Not dough dumplings.
Dumplings of the world.Kibbeh: A Levantine torpedo of bulgur and minced meat, usually fried. A dumpling of sorts, but its shell is bulgur, not dough.

Noodle dishes.Pad thai: Thailand's national noodle dish, promoted in the 1930s and 40s by Prime Minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram to build national identity and cut rice use.
Noodle dishes.Ramen: Japanese wheat noodles in broth. Alkaline kansui in the dough gives its springy bite and yellow color.
Noodle dishes.Pho: Vietnamese beef noodle soup with rice noodles, the best known export of Hanoi's street food.
Noodle dishes.Lo mein: Cantonese tossed egg noodles in sauce. The name means stirred noodles.
Noodle dishes.Chow mein: Stir-fried noodles whose name means fried noodles. In the US a crispy version is common, while in China it is usually soft.
Noodle dishes.Laksa: Spicy noodle soup from Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, in coconut or tamarind broth. Peranakan culture shaped it.
Noodle dishes.Japchae: Korean stir-fried glass noodles made from sweet potato starch. A royal court dish originally made with no noodles.
Noodle dishes.Dan dan noodles: Sichuan noodles with chili oil and sesame paste. They are named for the pole carried by street vendors.
Noodle dishes.Udon: Thick wheat noodles from Japan, often served in a simple hot dashi broth. Kagawa prefecture is known as udon prefecture.
Noodle dishes.Soba: Japanese buckwheat noodles. Eating them on New Year's Eve is a tradition meant to cut off the bad luck of the old year.
Noodle dishes.Pad see ew: Thai stir-fried wide rice noodles with dark soy sauce. The name means fried with soy sauce.
Noodle dishes.Yakisoba: Japanese stir-fried wheat noodles, ironically not made of buckwheat despite the name. It is a festival stall favorite.
Noodle dishes.Chow fun: Cantonese stir-fried wide rice noodles, famously cooked in a wok over high heat. That smoky flavor is called wok hei.
Noodle dishes.Risotto: Italian rice dish. It uses grains, not noodles.
Noodle dishes.Paella: Spanish rice dish whose crust is prized. No noodles are used, apart from fideua, a cousin.
Noodle dishes.Biryani: Layered spiced rice. Basmati grains, not noodles.
Noodle dishes.Fried rice: A way to use leftover rice. Day-old, drier grains fry better than fresh rice.
Noodle dishes.Congee: Rice porridge. The grains are cooked until they fall apart rather than shaped into noodles.
Noodle dishes.Bibimbap: Korean rice bowl topped with vegetables, meat and an egg. Its name means mixed rice.
Noodle dishes.Gyoza: Japanese dumplings, which are filled dough, not noodles.
Noodle dishes.Sushi: Vinegared rice with fish. Nothing here involves noodles.
Noodle dishes.Tempura: Batter-fried seafood and vegetables. Often served with soba, though, which is where the noodles come from.
Noodle dishes.Nasi goreng: Indonesian fried rice with sweet soy sauce. The name means fried rice. Mie goreng is its noodle twin.
Noodle dishes.Satay: Grilled skewers of marinated meat with peanut sauce. No noodles involved.

Whiskey cocktails.Old Fashioned: Sugar, bitters, whiskey and an orange twist; the name comes from 1880s drinkers who wanted their cocktail made the 'old-fashioned' way.
Whiskey cocktails.Manhattan: Rye or bourbon, sweet vermouth, and bitters. Legend ties it to a New York club in the 1870s, and it's named for the borough.
Whiskey cocktails.Whiskey sour: Whiskey, lemon, and sugar. Many bartenders add egg white, which gives a silky foam and a drink that is more than 150 years old.
Whiskey cocktails.Mint julep: Bourbon, mint, sugar, and crushed ice; the official drink of the Kentucky Derby, where over 120,000 are served each year.
Whiskey cocktails.Sazerac: Named for the Sazerac-de-Forge cognac first used; rye replaced it after phylloxera devastated French vineyards in the 1800s.
Whiskey cocktails.Irish coffee: Hot coffee, Irish whiskey, sugar, and cream. A Shannon Airport chef created it in the 1940s for chilled passengers, and a San Francisco bartender then spread it.
Whiskey cocktails.Boulevardier: A Negroni cousin made with bourbon or rye instead of gin. It was named for a Paris-based American writer who ran a magazine in the 1920s.
Whiskey cocktails.Rob Roy: Scotch, sweet vermouth, and bitters; a Manhattan with Scotch. It was named in 1894 for a Broadway operetta about the Scottish outlaw.
Whiskey cocktails.Penicillin: A modern classic from Sam Ross in New York, 2005: Scotch, lemon, honey-ginger syrup, and a float of smoky Islay whisky.
Whiskey cocktails.Rusty Nail: Scotch and Drambuie, a mix popular among 1960s celebrities. It's mixed with just two ingredients.
Whiskey cocktails.Paper Plane: Bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, and lemon in equal parts, created in 2008 by Sam Ross. The name was inspired by M.I.A.'s song.
Whiskey cocktails.Gold Rush: Bourbon, lemon, and honey syrup; a simple drink from New York in the 2000s. It's a whiskey Bee's Knees.
Whiskey cocktails.Margarita: A trap: it is tequila with lime and triple sec, often salt-rimmed. A rum cousin exists, but the classic never touches whiskey.
Whiskey cocktails.Paloma: A trap: tequila and grapefruit soda, with a pinch of salt. Mexico's most popular tequila drink has no whiskey in it.
Whiskey cocktails.Negroni: Equal parts gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth. It is gin-based, but the Boulevardier swaps in whiskey.
Whiskey cocktails.Mojito: Rum, mint, and lime. A Cuban classic that sometimes confuses with the Mint julep, but its base is rum.
Whiskey cocktails.Daiquiri: A trap: rum, lime, and sugar. Hemingway loved it, but it is a rum drink, with no whiskey anywhere, despite its sour structure.
Whiskey cocktails.Cosmopolitan: A trap: vodka, cranberry, lime, and triple sec. The pink drink of 1990s television is vodka-based, not whiskey.
Whiskey cocktails.Bloody Mary: A trap: vodka, tomato juice, and spices; sometimes fans make it with whiskey, called a Bloody Mick, but the classic uses vodka.
Whiskey cocktails.Piña colada: A trap: rum, coconut cream, and pineapple juice. Puerto Rico's national drink is tropical and rum-based, not whiskey.
Whiskey cocktails.Mai tai: A trap: it is rum, lime, orgeat, and orange curaçao. This tiki classic has nothing to do with whiskey.
Whiskey cocktails.Aperol spritz: A trap: Italy's bright orange aperitif is Aperol, prosecco, and soda, a light and bittersweet cocktail with no whiskey.
Whiskey cocktails.Sidecar: Cognac, orange liqueur, and lemon, with a sugared rim. It is one of the most beautiful brandy drinks, so no whiskey.
Whiskey cocktails.Gimlet: Gin and lime. A trap because it has the same simple style as a whiskey sour, but it's gin-based.

National capitals starting with B.Berlin: Germany's capital has been reunified since 1990, and it reportedly has more bridges than Venice.
National capitals starting with B.Bern: Switzerland's capital is officially called a federal city, not a capital, since the constitution names none.
National capitals starting with B.Brussels: Belgium's capital hosts the European Commission and NATO headquarters, and it is also bilingual.
National capitals starting with B.Budapest: Hungary's capital was once two cities, Buda and Pest, which merged in 1873.
National capitals starting with B.Bucharest: Romania's capital has the Palace of Parliament, one of the heaviest buildings in the world.
National capitals starting with B.Belgrade: Serbia's capital stands where the Sava meets the Danube, and it is one of Europe's oldest cities.
National capitals starting with B.Bratislava: Slovakia's capital sits on the Danube only about 60 km from Vienna, so two capitals are a short drive apart.
National capitals starting with B.Beijing: China's capital, whose name means northern capital, hosted both the summer and winter Olympics.
National capitals starting with B.Bangkok: Thailand's capital has a Thai name that is one of the longest city names in the world.
National capitals starting with B.Baghdad: Iraq's capital was founded in AD 762 as a round city and became a center of the Islamic Golden Age.
National capitals starting with B.Beirut: Lebanon's capital has been destroyed and rebuilt many times, and was once called the Paris of the Middle East.
National capitals starting with B.Bogotá: Colombia's capital sits high in the Andes at about 2,600 m.
National capitals starting with B.Buenos Aires: Argentina's capital is known for its tango and its elegant boulevards.
National capitals starting with B.Brasília: Brazil's purpose-built capital opened in 1960 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
National capitals starting with B.Barcelona: A trap. It is Spain's second city, the capital of Catalonia, but Madrid is the national capital.
National capitals starting with B.Bonn: It was West Germany's capital until 1990, and Beethoven was born there.
National capitals starting with B.Bordeaux: The French wine city is famous for its vineyards, but Paris is the capital.
National capitals starting with B.Birmingham: England's second city has more canals than Venice, but London is the capital.
National capitals starting with B.Bristol: The English port city was home of engineer Brunel and is not the capital.
National capitals starting with B.Basel: This Swiss city on the Rhine is a hub of pharmaceuticals and art fairs, but it is not the capital.
National capitals starting with B.Bologna: It is home to the oldest university in the world, founded in 1088, but not Italy's capital.
National capitals starting with B.Busan: South Korea's second city and biggest port, not the capital.
National capitals starting with B.Brisbane: The capital of Queensland, Australia's third-largest city, is not the national capital, Canberra.
National capitals starting with B.Bruges: Belgium's medieval city of canals is a tourist favorite, but the capital is Brussels.

Flags with green on them.Brazil: Its flag is mostly green with a yellow diamond. The green is said to stand for the forests and the yellow for gold.
Flags with green on them.Italy: Italy's tricolor was adopted in 1797 for a Napoleonic-era republic, and it gained its modern form in 1946 after the monarchy ended.
Flags with green on them.Ireland: The green stands for the Gaelic tradition, orange for the followers of William of Orange, and white for peace between them.
Flags with green on them.Mexico: A green, white and red tricolor with an eagle on a cactus. Green originally stood for independence.
Flags with green on them.Nigeria: Two green bands flank a white band, and the design was chosen in a 1959 competition, won by a student named Michael Taiwo Akinkunmi.
Flags with green on them.Saudi Arabia: A green field carrying the Islamic creed in white Arabic script and a sword. The green is linked with Islam.
Flags with green on them.Pakistan: Dark green stands for the Muslim majority, and the white stripe at the left for religious minorities.
Flags with green on them.Bangladesh: A deep green field with a red disc offset slightly toward the hoist so that it looks centered when flying.
Flags with green on them.India: The saffron, white and green tricolor has a green band at the bottom, standing for faith and fertility of the land.
Flags with green on them.Portugal: The green and red flag was adopted in 1911 after the monarchy fell. Green replaced the traditional blue and white.
Flags with green on them.South Africa: Its 1994 flag has a Y-shaped green band. The colors blend ones from many parties and traditions, and it's one of the most colorful flags.
Flags with green on them.Kenya: Black, red, and green bands with a Maasai shield and spears in the center. Green stands for the land.
Flags with green on them.Jamaica: The only flag in the world with no red, white or blue. Gold, black and green make up its saltire.
Flags with green on them.France: Blue, white and red. Not one drop of green, which is true for most European tricolors.
Flags with green on them.Germany: Black, red and gold, so no green at all, despite its forests.
Flags with green on them.Japan: A red sun on white, with no green anywhere. Green gets a nod only in Japan's old imperial colors and in the green of its famous matcha.
Flags with green on them.USA: Red, white and blue with white stars, and no green, despite the dollar's famous color.
Flags with green on them.UK: The Union Flag has red, white and blue only. Wales' dragon flag has green, but the Welsh dragon isn't included in the Union Flag.
Flags with green on them.Russia: White, blue and red horizontal bands with no green. Its colors come from Peter the Great's time.
Flags with green on them.Canada: Only red and white, though the leaf is famously green in summer. Red and white were declared national colors by George V in 1921.
Flags with green on them.Sweden: Blue and yellow only. The colors come from the royal coat of arms.
Flags with green on them.Argentina: Light blue and white bands with a golden sun, so no green.
Flags with green on them.Poland: White over red only, and no green at all. Those colors have marked Polish heraldry since the Middle Ages, from the white eagle on a red field.
Flags with green on them.Netherlands: Red, white and blue stripes. No green despite the grassy polders.

Women in science.Marie Curie: First woman to win a Nobel Prize and still the only person honored in two different sciences, for physics and for chemistry.
Women in science.Rosalind Franklin: Her X-ray photograph, Photo 51, revealed the helical shape of DNA, but she died before the 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery.
Women in science.Ada Lovelace: Wrote the notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine that include what's often called the first computer program, back in the 1840s.
Women in science.Jane Goodall: Her patient fieldwork showed chimpanzees make tools, and she turned from research into a global voice for conservation.
Women in science.Rachel Carson: A marine biologist whose book Silent Spring exposed the damage of DDT and sparked the modern environmental movement.
Women in science.Lise Meitner: She helped explain nuclear fission in 1938, yet the Nobel went to her colleague alone. Element 109, meitnerium, honors her.
Women in science.Dorothy Hodgkin: She decoded the molecular structure of penicillin and insulin and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964.
Women in science.Vera Rubin: Her galaxy measurements gave strong evidence for dark matter, but she never received a Nobel Prize.
Women in science.Grace Hopper: A US Navy rear admiral who helped create COBOL, an early programming language, and popularized the term debugging after a real moth was found in a computer.
Women in science.Katherine Johnson: A NASA mathematician whose orbital calculations helped launch Americans into space. Astronaut John Glenn asked her to verify the computer's numbers by hand.
Women in science.Hedy Lamarr: A Hollywood star who co-invented frequency hopping, an idea behind modern Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, during World War Two.
Women in science.Barbara McClintock: She discovered jumping genes in corn, which was ignored for decades before she won the 1983 Nobel Prize.
Women in science.Mae Jemison: In 1992 she became the first Black woman in space, and she later left NASA to run a science education effort.
Women in science.Chien-Shiung Wu: Nicknamed the First Lady of Physics, she disproved the idea that nature is mirror-symmetric, but the 1957 Nobel went to her male colleagues.
Women in science.Niels Bohr: Danish quantum pioneer whose Copenhagen institute drew the era's best minds. He's a great physicist but a man, so he's off a list of women.
Women in science.Enrico Fermi: He built the first nuclear reactor in 1942 and has element 100 named for him, but as a man he doesn't fit this list of women.
Women in science.Alan Turing: He cracked Enigma and sketched the modern computer, but he's a man, so the list of women scientists leaves him out.
Women in science.Edwin Hubble: The Hubble telescope carries his name, but he's a man. The distance yardstick he relied on came from Henrietta Leavitt.
Women in science.Carl Sagan: He brought astronomy to millions through Cosmos, but he's a man, so he isn't one of the women scientists here.
Women in science.Linus Pauling: He won two Nobel Prizes, chemistry and peace, but as a man he's not part of this list of women.
Women in science.Gregor Mendel: He founded genetics by breeding peas in a monastery garden, but he's a man, so he's out of this list.
Women in science.Louis Pasteur: He developed pasteurization and vaccines for rabies and anthrax, but as a man he's not on the women-in-science list.
Women in science.Max Planck: He launched quantum theory in 1900 with the idea of energy packets, but he's a man, so he doesn't fit here.
Women in science.Paul Dirac: His 1928 equation predicted antimatter, but he's a man, so he isn't on a list of women in science.

Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Cambrian: About 540 million years ago, life suddenly diversified in the 'Cambrian explosion', and most major animal groups appeared in the fossil record.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Ordovician: Ended with the second-largest mass extinction, around 445 million years ago, probably triggered by glaciation and falling seas.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Silurian: Named for the Silures, an ancient Welsh tribe. In this period, plants and animals first began to colonize dry land in numbers.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Devonian: The 'Age of Fishes', named for Devon, England. Early four-legged animals crawled out of the water, and the first forests grew.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Carboniferous: Its name means 'coal-bearing': its swampy forests became much of the world's coal. Giant dragonflies with wings near 70 cm flew in it.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Permian: Ended with the worst extinction ever, the 'Great Dying', about 252 million years ago, which wiped out over 90 percent of marine species.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Triassic: The age when dinosaurs and the first mammals appeared. It began after the Great Dying and ended with another extinction.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Jurassic: Named for the Jura Mountains, not for the movies. It's when giants like Brachiosaurus roamed and the first birds appeared.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Cretaceous: Name comes from the Latin for chalk, as the White Cliffs of Dover formed then. It ended about 66 million years ago, when an asteroid hit.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Paleogene: The period right after the dinosaurs died off, when mammals diversified into whales, horses and primates. It lasted about 43 million years.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Quaternary: The period we live in now, from about 2.6 million years ago. It includes the ice ages and the whole of human history.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Mesozoic: A trap: this is an era, not a period. The 'Age of Reptiles' holds three periods: Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Paleozoic: An era, not a period, spanning the Cambrian through the Permian. Its name means 'ancient life'.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Cenozoic: Our current era, the 'Age of Mammals', which began 66 million years ago. It contains the Paleogene, Neogene and Quaternary periods.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Pleistocene: An epoch, not a period: the part of the Quaternary famous for ice ages, mammoths and saber-toothed cats.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Holocene: The epoch we live in, which started about 11,700 years ago when the last ice age ended. All of recorded history fits inside it.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Ice Age: Not an official time unit. Because Earth still has polar ice caps, we are technically still in an ice age, in a warmer spell between glaciations.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Bronze Age: A span of human culture, not geology, which began around 3300 BCE in places. Bronze, a copper and tin alloy, gave it its name.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Stone Age: Humans used stone tools for roughly 3 million years. It's an archaeological label rather than a geologic period.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Iron Age: A human cultural stage, not a geologic one. Iron tools beat bronze since iron ore is far more common than tin.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Renaissance: A cultural movement, not a geologic period. It began in 14th-century Italy and means 'rebirth'.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Victorian: A period of British history named for Queen Victoria, who reigned from 1837 to 1901. Nothing geologic about it.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Precambrian: A trap: it covers the 88 percent of Earth's history before the Cambrian, an informal span rather than a single period.
Geologic periods (not eras or epochs).Archean: An eon, not a period, from about 4 to 2.5 billion years ago. The first single-celled life appeared in it.

Real chemical element symbols.He: Helium was spotted in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, years before anyone found it on Earth, and its name comes from the Greek for the Sun.
Real chemical element symbols.Ne: Neon glows reddish-orange in a tube, and most coloured 'neon' signs actually use other gases or phosphor coatings.
Real chemical element symbols.Ar: Argon makes up about 1% of the air, the third most common gas, and its name means 'lazy' in Greek because it hardly reacts.
Real chemical element symbols.Kr: Krypton means 'hidden'; from 1960 to 1983, the metre was officially defined using the orange light of one of its isotopes.
Real chemical element symbols.Xe: Xenon means 'stranger'; it fills some car headlights and is used as propellant in ion engines on spacecraft.
Real chemical element symbols.Fe: Fe comes from the Latin ferrum, and most of Earth's core is thought to be made of iron.
Real chemical element symbols.Au: Au comes from Latin aurum, and all the gold ever mined would fit in a cube roughly 20 metres on a side.
Real chemical element symbols.Ag: Ag comes from Latin argentum, and silver is the best electrical conductor of all the metals.
Real chemical element symbols.Pb: Pb comes from Latin plumbum, which also gave us 'plumber' since Roman water pipes were made of lead.
Real chemical element symbols.Sn: Sn comes from Latin stannum, and mixing tin with copper produced bronze, which gave a whole age its name.
Real chemical element symbols.Hg: Hg is from hydrargyrum, 'liquid silver'; mercury is the only metal that is liquid at ordinary room temperature.
Real chemical element symbols.Na: Na comes from natrium, and sodium reacts so fiercely with water that it is stored under oil.
Real chemical element symbols.Zn: Zn stands for zinc, which, blended with copper, makes brass.
Real chemical element symbols.Cu: Cu comes from Latin cuprum, 'metal of Cyprus', the island famous for its ancient copper mines.
Real chemical element symbols.Jo: No element symbol uses the letter J, so a name-like pair such as Jo can never appear on the periodic table.
Real chemical element symbols.Qu: The letter Q appears in no element symbol at all, so Qu is out.
Real chemical element symbols.Ma: Not a symbol; magnesium is Mg and manganese is Mn, while Ma sits in no cell of the table.
Real chemical element symbols.Ea: No element begins with Ea; the nearest are einsteinium (Es) and europium (Eu).
Real chemical element symbols.Ox: Oxygen's symbol is just O; a second letter is only added when the single letter is taken, so Ox does not exist.
Real chemical element symbols.Ty: Not an element; titanium is Ti, and thallium is Tl.
Real chemical element symbols.Gl: No element symbol starts with Gl; the real G-elements are Ga, Gd and Ge.
Real chemical element symbols.Me: Me is not an element, though chemists do use it as shorthand for a methyl group in diagrams.
Real chemical element symbols.Ab: Ab is not a real symbol; actinium is Ac, and no symbol begins with Ab.
Real chemical element symbols.Le: Le is not an element; lithium is Li and livermorium is Lv.

Spells from Harry Potter.Expelliarmus: The disarming charm is Harry's signature spell; it was the one he used in his last duel with Voldemort, whose own curse rebounded.
Spells from Harry Potter.Lumos: Lights the wand tip, from Latin lumen, light. Its opposite, Nox, snuffs the glow out again.
Spells from Harry Potter.Accio: The summoning charm, Latin for I summon. Harry used it on his broomstick, the Firebolt, to win the Triwizard Tournament's dragon task.
Spells from Harry Potter.Wingardium Leviosa: Hermione's lesson to Ron: it's Levi-O-sa, not Levio-SAR. Ron used the levitation charm to drop a troll's club on its owner.
Spells from Harry Potter.Expecto Patronum: Conjures a guardian that repels Dementors, and its shape is unique to each wizard. Harry's is a stag, like his father's.
Spells from Harry Potter.Alohomora: The unlocking charm; Hermione used it to open the forbidden third-floor door that hid the giant three-headed dog.
Spells from Harry Potter.Avada Kedavra: The Killing Curse, one of three Unforgivables. Rowling said it echoes an ancient Aramaic phrase behind abracadabra, meaning let the thing be destroyed.
Spells from Harry Potter.Stupefy: The Stunning Spell knocks its target out cold, and it is the workhorse of nearly every wizard duel in the books.
Spells from Harry Potter.Obliviate: The memory charm. Gilderoy Lockhart tried it with Ron's broken wand, and it backfired and wiped out his own memory.
Spells from Harry Potter.Riddikulus: Defeats a boggart by turning your fear into something funny. Neville's version put his scary teacher Snape in his grandmother's clothes.
Spells from Harry Potter.Nox: The counter-spell to Lumos, which extinguishes the wand's light. It's Latin for night.
Spells from Harry Potter.Reparo: Mends broken objects, from Latin for repair. Hermione used it to fix Harry's cracked glasses on the Hogwarts Express.
Spells from Harry Potter.Abracadabra: A real old charm, not a Harry Potter spell. In ancient Rome it was written on amulets worn against fever, in a shrinking triangle.
Spells from Harry Potter.Hocus Pocus: Stage-magician patter from 17th-century England, possibly a mock of the Latin Mass. It's a Halloween film title, not a Hogwarts spell.
Spells from Harry Potter.Bibbidi-Bobbidi-Boo: The Fairy Godmother's chant in Disney's Cinderella (1950). The song was nominated for the Best Original Song Oscar.
Spells from Harry Potter.Open Sesame: Ali Baba's password to the thieves' cave in the Arabian Nights. Ripe sesame pods pop open, a likely inspiration for the phrase.
Spells from Harry Potter.Shazam: Saying it turns Billy Batson into a superhero. The word stands for six legendary figures, among them Solomon, Hercules and Zeus.
Spells from Harry Potter.Alakazam: A stage-magic cry, and also the name of a psychic Pokemon that Kadabra evolves into. It was never cast at Hogwarts.
Spells from Harry Potter.Sim Sala Bim: The catchphrase of the stage magician Dante, whose touring revue by that name reached Broadway in 1940. Not a wizarding spell.
Spells from Harry Potter.Presto: Italian for quick, and the magician's word for the instant the trick lands. Pixar also made a short film called Presto about a magician's rabbit.
Spells from Harry Potter.Hakuna Matata: Swahili for no worries, made worldwide famous by The Lion King. It's a motto, not a magic word.
Spells from Harry Potter.Klaatu Barada Nikto: The words that stop the robot Gort in the 1951 sci-fi film The Day the Earth Stood Still. A command to a robot, not a spell.
Spells from Harry Potter.Engage: Captain Picard's famous order to the helmsman in Star Trek: The Next Generation, not a Hogwarts spell.
Spells from Harry Potter.Cowabunga: Surfer slang popularized by Chief Thunderthud on Howdy Doody, then by the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. No wizard has cast it.

Science fiction TV series.Star Trek: The original 1966 series ran only three seasons, and fans' letter-writing campaigns helped save it from cancellation after season two.
Science fiction TV series.Doctor Who: The longest-running sci-fi show ever, on air since 1963. The Doctor's regeneration was invented to keep the show going when the first star, William Hartnell, left.
Science fiction TV series.The X-Files: Chris Carter's show about FBI agents Mulder and Scully made the line The Truth Is Out There famous. It premiered in 1993 and returned in revival seasons.
Science fiction TV series.Battlestar Galactica: The 2004 reboot of a 1978 series. Its Cylons could look human, and critics praised it for treating war and politics seriously.
Science fiction TV series.Firefly: Fox made only 14 episodes in 2002 before canceling it, yet fan devotion won it a 2005 film, Serenity.
Science fiction TV series.Stranger Things: Set in 1980s Indiana, its logo was inspired by Stephen King paperbacks. Season four sent Kate Bush's Running Up That Hill back up the charts in 2022.
Science fiction TV series.Black Mirror: Charlie Brooker's anthology about technology's dark side began on Britain's Channel 4 before Netflix took over. Each episode has a new cast and world.
Science fiction TV series.The Twilight Zone: Rod Serling hosted this 1959 anthology and wrote most of its episodes. It made the twist ending a TV staple.
Science fiction TV series.Westworld: Based on Michael Crichton's 1973 film, HBO's version follows lifelike androids in a theme park. The maze at its heart symbolizes awakening consciousness.
Science fiction TV series.The Expanse: Adapted from James S. A. Corey's novels, it began on Syfy, and Amazon revived it after cancellation. Fans praised its careful treatment of zero gravity.
Science fiction TV series.Severance: At Lumon, workers have their memories split between office and home. The cold corridors were filmed at Bell Works, a former Bell Labs building in New Jersey.
Science fiction TV series.Andor: A Star Wars prequel to Rogue One, written for adults. Critics praised how it shows the Empire as a bureaucracy as much as an army.
Science fiction TV series.The Mandalorian: The first live-action Star Wars series launched Disney+ in 2019. Its tiny green star, Grogu, was kept secret until the first episode aired.
Science fiction TV series.Mad Men: Set at a 1960s Madison Avenue ad agency, it is a period drama, not sci-fi. It won the Emmy for best drama four years in a row.
Science fiction TV series.The Wire: A crime drama about Baltimore by David Simon, a former police reporter for the Baltimore Sun. Each season explores a different part of the city.
Science fiction TV series.Friends: A sitcom about six friends in New York, in the realistic comedy genre. Its 2004 finale drew about 52 million US viewers.
Science fiction TV series.Seinfeld: Co-created by Larry David, this sitcom was famously about nothing and never involved science fiction. Its 1998 finale drew about 76 million US viewers.
Science fiction TV series.The Crown: A Netflix drama about Queen Elizabeth II's reign. Its main cast changed every two seasons so the characters could age on screen.
Science fiction TV series.Downton Abbey: A period drama about an English country house, filmed at Highclere Castle. It's history, not speculative fiction.
Science fiction TV series.Succession: A drama about a media dynasty, partly inspired by families like the Murdochs. It's a family drama, not a sci-fi series.
Science fiction TV series.Grey's Anatomy: A medical drama set in Seattle that premiered in 2005. It has outlasted most other US primetime dramas, but it has no futuristic elements.
Science fiction TV series.Suits: A legal drama set in New York. Meghan Markle played paralegal Rachel Zane, and it found new fans when it hit Netflix years after ending.
Science fiction TV series.Cheers: A Boston bar sitcom, 1982 to 1993, that spawned Frasier. It's a comedy set in the real world.
Science fiction TV series.The Sopranos: A mob drama about a New Jersey boss in therapy. It's a crime series, and its sudden cut to black in 2007 is still debated.

Things with strings.Marionette: Pulled from above, it takes its name from the French for little Mary. Skilled puppeteers can make one seem alive.
Things with strings.Kite: Chinese kites date back over 2,000 years, and early ones were used to send signals and measure distances.
Things with strings.Tennis racket: Pros often string theirs at 50 to 60 pounds of tension, and restring often because the strings lose their snap.
Things with strings.Violin: Its four strings are tuned in fifths and its bow is strung with horsehair, usually from the tail of a horse.
Things with strings.Archery bow: Bow strings store energy from the bent limbs, and a target archer's bow often draws about 40 pounds.
Things with strings.Yo-yo: The Philippines gave the toy its name, and Pedro Flores sold it in the US from the 1920s before it was a craze.
Things with strings.Guitar: Strings were once made from sheep gut, but nylon and steel took over.
Things with strings.Harp: Ireland uses a harp as its national emblem, and it is on the back of Irish euro coins.
Things with strings.Banjo: Its drum-like skin body gives that twang, and the roots lie in West African instruments.
Things with strings.Badminton racket: A smash can fly at over 400 km/h, the fastest speed of any racket sport. The racket is light but strung tight.
Things with strings.Lute: The ancestor of the guitar, its name comes from the Arabic al-ud, and it was a star of the Renaissance.
Things with strings.Drum: Snare drums have metal wires under the bottom head, but they rattle against it and are not played, so it is not a stringed instrument.
Things with strings.Trumpet: Brass instrument. Its sound comes from the player's buzzing lips, not strings.
Things with strings.Flute: Sound comes from air splitting over an edge. The flute is a player's breath, not strings.
Things with strings.Football: American footballs have laces, but those aren't strings you play or pull.
Things with strings.Golf club: Until the mid-1800s, golf balls were leather pouches stuffed with feathers.
Things with strings.Frisbee: Often said to be inspired by pie tins from the Frisbie Baking Company, it flies on lift, not strings.
Things with strings.Skateboard: Born when surfers wanted something to ride on the sidewalk in 1950s California.
Things with strings.Saxophone: Invented by Adolphe Sax in the 1840s, it is brass but counts as woodwind because of its single reed.
Things with strings.Hula hoop: The craze of 1958 sold tens of millions in months, and nothing to string.
Things with strings.Cricket bat: Made from willow, and no strings attached, just a wooden blade.
Things with strings.Xylophone: Wooden bars and mallets. Unlike a piano, which hammers strings, the xylophone has none.
Things with strings.Bagpipes: Reeds and drone pipes, fed by a bag of air. No strings.
Things with strings.Kazoo: A membrane that buzzes when you hum, so it has no strings.
